title: Quality IMAP, Part 2: Mailbox Concurrency
excerpt: An open-source distributed storage service you can self-host to fullfill many needs.
content_html:
In the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the second part in a series discussing why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and presenting our work on making Aerogramme's IMAP code as high-quality as we can. Today we focus on challenges that arise when considering concurrent access to a mailbox.

Aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network issues and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

This is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement. In the previous post, we talked about the first class of features: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents. In this post, we talk about the second class of features that make implementing an IMAP server tricky: concurrent access to user mailboxes.

Concurrent and distributed software are famously hard to get right; concurrency bugs are known to be hard to find. In our recent work on refining Aerogramme we have tried to approach the problem from different angles. This is the topic of this post: the different ways in which we have improved the correctness of Aerogramme in concurrent settings.

This work was funded by NLNet under the "Aerogramme 1.0" grant, and could not have been possible without their support.

Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat!

Concurrent mailbox access in IMAP

A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox. For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer. Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing. In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes.

Why must clients be able to coordinate when accessing the same mailbox? Assume that we are an email client that sends two commands to read information from a mailbox. Since another client can modify the mailbox in between the two commands, the information we read may have been invalidated by the other client and is now inconsistent! Clients thus need to be able to detect concurrent changes made by other clients. Similarly, a client that reconnects to the server after being offline needs to fetch the changes that happened while it was disconnected. This is possible thanks to mechanisms defined by the IMAP specification and that specifically exist because concurrent access is allowed.

The overall consistency of the mailbox data must be taken seriously: an IMAP server exposing inconsistent views of a mailbox could result in a confused client deleting the wrong emails, for example.

To our best knowledge, concurrent mailbox behaviors are tackled in the following (parts of) specifications:

Base IMAP

The base IMAP4 specification has few explicit mentions of concurrent mailbox access, but does talk about re-synchronizing disconnected clients, which can be seen as a restricted form of concurrent access. It defines mechanisms for assigning IDs to emails (UIDNEXT/UIDVALIDITY) and associated properties which can be extrapolated to concurrent contexts. This is relevant when concurrently adding new emails to a mailbox. After an email has been added to a mailbox it cannot be modified, so there are no issues with reading emails concurrently.

The improvements that we will talk about in this post are related to these aspects of the base IMAP specification.

As an additional complication, IMAP defines in fact two (!) email-numbering systems. One of these has the drawback that deleting an email can invalidate email IDs used in concurrent commands. This is purely a quirk of a numbering system that can nowadays be considered legacy, but must still be supported. This issue is not acknowledged in the base IMAP specification, leaving a class of problematic behaviors completely unspecified, but is later addressed in an informational RFC which specifies what to do in such cases.

Aerogramme's latest release includes changes and bugfixes to make sure that we follow the recommendations of this informational RFC, but we won't enter into the details of these legacy quirks in this post.

Extensions

Email flags can be modified concurrently, but the base IMAP specification does not specify a mechanism for clients to coordinate around flag changes. This is done in the later CONDSTORE specification that extends IMAP with mechanisms to coordinate flag changes across concurrent connections. Aerogramme has preliminary support for CONDSTORE, but we disabled it in the last release, as we found out it needs a redesign to be nicer to email clients1.

A later specification further extends IMAP and CONDSTORE by adding a more general mechanism (QRESYNC) for synchronizing all mailbox changes across concurrent sessions. Aerogramme does not supports QRESYNC at the moment2.

Context: Concurrency in Aerogramme

On top of the complexity carried by the IMAP specification, Aerogramme's distributed infrastructure comes with its own challenges. Not only we need to think about concurrency at the IMAP protocol level, but also internally in Aerogramme: how do we handle concurrent changes to the server internal data storage? Can we simply take a lock or a transaction over mailbox data each time we need to update it, serializing all concurrent updates? The answer is no: things are a bit more complicated...

Recall that Aerogramme is a distributed IMAP server. A typical Aerogramme deployment looks like this:

In this schema, A nodes are Aerogramme instances running on separate servers. Running multiple Aerogramme nodes provides fault-tolerance: even if some of the nodes crash, the Aerogramme cluster stays operational as long as one node remains available. When an email client (a C node) connects to the "Aerogramme cluster" (the dashed potato), it can open a connection to any of the Aerogramme nodes, depending on what kind of load-balancing is implemented.

Aerogramme nodes do not talk to each other directly and do not store data themselves. Instead, they connect a shared Garage cluster (itself geo-distributed with fault-tolerance properties) which stores data for the whole Aerogramme cluster (emails, mailbox state, etc.).

This means that an Aerogramme node deals with concurrency at two levels. It must handle concurrent connections from email clients to a mailbox, as we explained before. But it must also handle concurrent changes made by other Aerogramme nodes to the data stored in Garage. These concurrent accesses must be coordinated properly so that the Aerogramme cluster exposes a consistent view of a mailbox (according to IMAP's consistency requirements), even when connecting concurrently to different nodes of the Aerogramme cluster.

A central challenge in Aerogramme's design is that Garage does not provide locks, transactions, or anything that would require distributed consensus between Garage nodes. This is by design, and it allows Garage and Aerogramme to perform well even with non-negligible latency between nodes. The consequence for Aerogramme is that its nodes cannot simply reason on their shared data as if it was updated sequentially. The approach used by Aerogramme instead—a convergent operation log—is a central part of its design. We'll talk more below on how we adjusted the consistency properties provided by Garage when storing that operation log.

Testing the consistency of email numbering in Aerogramme

A basic IMAP mechanism is assigning IDs to emails when they are added into a mailbox. Adding emails concurrently can already make it tricky to assign these IDs. Our first step was to find a way of testing this case and to fix any bugs that we would find.

For context, IMAP specifies that each email in a mailbox must be assigned a UID: a number that identifies it uniquely. UIDs are assigned in increasing order; this allows clients to check if new emails have been added by checking the value of the mailbox "next UID". On top of that, IMAP also allows the server to renumber the emails with different UIDs. When this happens, the IMAP server must increase the value of UIDVALIDITY, a global integer counter attached to the mailbox. Now, in Aerogramme, increasing UIDVALIDITY is done in some cases when emails are added concurrently in the mailbox in a way that would assign conflicting UIDs; an unavoidable consequence of its distributed architecture.

From an IMAP client's perspective UIDVALIDITY must always increase monotonically. We also assume that this property must hold across all concurrent connections; although the specification does not say so explicitly, it is the most prudent assumption since a single client may open multiple connections to the same mailbox.

The logical next step is to setup a test bench to ensure that it holds in practice for Aerogramme! We deployed an Aerogramme cluster with three nodes, running on a simulated network with added latency between nodes. Then:

  • we run two processes concurrently adding emails to a test mailbox, from two different nodes of the cluster. This is enough to trigger UID assignation conflicts, forcing Aerogramme to renumber emails and increase UIDVALIDITY;
  • at the same time, we run a checker for our property: a program that reads UIDVALIDITY from two different nodes of the cluster and checks that the second value read is greater or equal to the first one.

Running Aerogramme on this test bench found state synchronization bugs: bugs showing that Aerogramme’s distributed state (stored in Garage) was not always properly synchronized between nodes and concurrent sessions. Amusingly, most of these bugs were not specific to the IMAP logic related to UIDVALIDITY...

Fixing these synchronization bugs motivated a redesign of the internal read/update mailbox interface. In Aerogramme, the IMAP "business logic" accesses mailbox state stored in distributed storage using an abstract interface exposing a small number of operations. Before, these operations were the following (in pseudo-Rust):

// `self` is a handle to the storage backend for a mailbox.

/// Read the current state of the mailbox from remote storage.
fn get(&self) -> State

/// Push an operation that updates the mailbox to remote storage.
fn push_op(&self, op: Operation)

The synchronization bugs found during testing revealed that this interface is in fact error-prone and tricky to reason about:

  1. get could return outdated values; this is because rebuilding mailbox state from remote storage can be expensive, so get internally maintained a cache which could get stale;
  2. doing let s1 = mailbox.get(); ...; let s2 = mailbox.get(); is a trap. In this case, s2 imports unknown operations pushed concurrently from other clients. In most cases this is not what we want, as IMAP commands must generally behave as if they operated on a "snapshot" of the mailbox taken as a single point in time;
  3. push_op modifies the state, but if we need the mailbox state with the operation we just pushed, we have to call get (and thus likely fall into the trap described in 2.).

The solution was to redesign Aerogramme's mailbox state interface to provide more control over state synchronization: reading concurrent changes from storage becomes a separate operation, laying the following interface:

// `self` is now a thread-local view of the state of a mailbox.
// It is local to a given client connection.
// (As an optimization, it internally pools ressources with other
// views of the same mailbox.)

/// Return the local view of the mailbox maintained by `self`.
/// Does not read remote storage.
fn get(&self) -> State

/// Push an operation that updates the mailbox.
/// Update both the local view and remote storage.
fn push_op(&mut self, op: Operation)

/// Synchronize the local view of the mailbox.
/// Read remote storage and imports all changes into the local view. 
fn sync(&mut self)

This new interface separates local reasoning about mailbox contents from synchronization. This makes it easier to write the IMAP logic in a way that is "obviously correct". Plainly speaking, this interface provides "local" views of mailbox state, where a view (denoted as self above) is specific to a client connection. Then, get and push_op operate on the local view with sequential semantics and are both fast; and calls to sync mark explicitly the places in the code where we have to think about concurrent changes. (Note that push_op synchronously updates remote storage, so there is no risk of losing write by forgetting to run sync.)

Notice that the design of this interface reflects the high-level distributed architecture that we described in the previous section. For instance, an implementation of the interface needs to "merge" the operations pushed concurrently with push_op when they are put together in distributed storage, in a way that is consistent with local views; this is backed by the "convergent operation log" mentioned earlier and domain-specific logic3. Note that this interface offers no transactional or lock-like operations; matching Garage's lack of consistency primitives.

Most of the changes described here were part of Aerogramme 0.4, with in particular #129 implementing the refactoring of the state synchronization interface.

"Monotonic Reads" Consistency for Garage K2V

Talking about consistency guarantees in Aerogramme raises the question: what are the consistency guarantees provided by Garage, its storage backend?

This question is most relevant for Garage K2V, a NoSQL-inspired key-value store, which is used to store mailbox state as an operation log. (Garage K2V is experimental and was added in Garage for the needs of Aerogramme.) Mailbox state describes (among other things) email numbering, and as we've seen before, we want this information to be properly synchronized between Aerogramme nodes.

Garage K2V provides read-after-write consistency4: this guarantees that as soon as a write is acknowledged by Garage, any subsequent read will see the update made by the write. In terms of Aerogramme's state synchronization interface, after running push_op(op);, this guarantees that sync(); get() returns a state that includes op on any Aerogramme node.

However, it turns out that read-after-write consistency alone is not enough for Aerogramme. Let's think of the fact that UIDVALIDITY needs to increase monotonically according to the IMAP specification. This means that calling sync(); get() twice on any two Aerogramme nodes must return a state that is more recent the second time than the first. In other words, when making several reads to Garage K2V in sequence, we must not see time go backward. This means that, to ensure consistency of the UIDVALIDITY counter, Aerogramme needs Garage K2V to guarantee an additional consistency property called monotonic reads!

As a result we have extended Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads consistency. Luckily, the design of Garage makes it possible to provide monotonic reads at only a small performance cost. For a reference, Martin Kleppmann's Designing data-intensive applications (in particular Chapter 9, "Linearizability and quorums") helps understanding which scenarios lead to non-monotonic reads in a quorum-based architecture like Garage's, and what to implement to guarantee monotonic reads.

To experimentally validate our changes, we first built a test bench that triggers non-monotonic reads on stock K2V. Reproducing non-monotonic reads requires variable network delays, so we deployed a Garage cluster with 3 nodes, on a simulated network with delay between cluster nodes. This test setup allows observing non-monotonic reads, by running:

  • a writer program that writes increasing integer values (0, 1, 2, etc.);
  • a reader program that performs two reads in sequence from two different nodes of the cluster, and checks that it reads an integer that is greater on the second read than on the first read.

We then modified Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads by default, by implementing "synchronous read repair". We validated that we cannot observe non-monotonic reads anymore on our test bench, while they could be observed before this change: a good sanity check.

This change in Garage K2V ensures that there are no scenarios in which a precise combination of network delays in the cluster results in an IMAP client observing non-increasing values of UIDVALIDITY. One could argue that this is unlikely to happen in practice; and indeed, we could not reproduce it with our simple-minded test bench: while we could observe non-monotonic reads with Garage K2V alone, we could not observe non-monotonic UIDVALIDITY on a full Garage+Aerogramme deployment with the same testing methodology. Nevertheless, we want Aerogramme to rest on strong, correct foundations as much as possible; eliminating a rare but possible cause of bugs was fully worth the effort.

The work described here was made available as part of Garage 2.4.0; it required no specific change in Aerogramme itself.

We designed Aerogramme to be part of a low-tech computing stack meant to be robust and reliable when hosted outside of data-centers, and Aerogramme's geo-distributed design is part of the answer. In the future, we hope to expand on the values and high-level ideas behind Aerogramme; this will have to be for an other blogpost...

1

The current implementation (now gated by a feature flag disabled by default) tends to disconnect clients more often than reasonable. This is correct with respect to the specification, but likely leads to bad UX in clients. We are working on a better strategy that does not require disconnecting clients.

2

The first step would be to gather data on how many clients actually support QRESYNC today...

3

We have not shown this "domain specific" merge logic (here, mailbox-specific) because it is a whole different topic, but it needs to be provided when instantiating the generic interface shown before with concrete state and operations.

4

read-after-write consistency is also the key consistency guarantee provided by Garage S3.

blocks.html_en: Concurrent mailbox access in IMAP

sentences.en: Concurrent mailbox access in IMAP

blocks.html_en: A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox. For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer. Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing. In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes.

sentences.en: A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox.
For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer.
Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing.
In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes.

blocks.html_en: Why must clients be able to coordinate when accessing the same mailbox? Assume that we are an email client that sends two commands to read information from a mailbox. Since another client can modify the mailbox in between the two commands, the information we read may have been invalidated by the other client and is now inconsistent! Clients thus need to be able to detect concurrent changes made by other clients. Similarly, a client that reconnects to the server after being offline needs to fetch the changes that happened while it was disconnected. This is possible thanks to mechanisms defined by the IMAP specification and that specifically exist because concurrent access is allowed.

blocks.html_en: The base IMAP4 specification has few explicit mentions of concurrent mailbox access, but does talk about re-synchronizing disconnected clients, which can be seen as a restricted form of concurrent access. blocks.html_en: For context, IMAP specifies that each email in a mailbox must be assigned a UID: a number that identifies it uniquely. UIDs are assigned in increasing order; this allows clients to check if new emails have been added by checking the value of the mailbox "next UID". On top of that, IMAP also allows the server to renumber the emails with different UIDs. When this happens, the IMAP server must increase the value of UIDVALIDITY, a global integer counter attached to the mailbox. Now, in Aerogramme, increasing UIDVALIDITY is done in some cases when emails are added concurrently in the mailbox in a way that would assign conflicting UIDs; an unavoidable consequence of its distributed architecture.

content_html_zh:
In the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the second part in a series discussing why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and presenting our work on making Aerogramme's IMAP code as high-quality as we can. Today we focus on challenges that arise when considering concurrent access to a mailbox.

Aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network issues and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

This is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement. In the previous post, we talked about the first class of features: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents. In this post, we talk about the second class of features that make implementing an IMAP server tricky: concurrent access to user mailboxes.

Concurrent and distributed software are famously hard to get right; concurrency bugs are known to be hard to find. In our recent work on refining Aerogramme we have tried to approach the problem from different angles. This is the topic of this post: the different ways in which we have improved the correctness of Aerogramme in concurrent settings.

This work was funded by NLNet under the "Aerogramme 1.0" grant, and could not have been possible without their support.

Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat!

Concurrent mailbox access in IMAP

A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox. For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer. Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing. In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes.

Why must clients be able to coordinate when accessing the same mailbox? Assume that we are an email client that sends two commands to read information from a mailbox. Since another client can modify the mailbox in between the two commands, the information we read may have been invalidated by the other client and is now inconsistent! Clients thus need to be able to detect concurrent changes made by other clients. Similarly, a client that reconnects to the server after being offline needs to fetch the changes that happened while it was disconnected. This is possible thanks to mechanisms defined by the IMAP specification and that specifically exist because concurrent access is allowed.

The overall consistency of the mailbox data must be taken seriously: an IMAP server exposing inconsistent views of a mailbox could result in a confused client deleting the wrong emails, for example.

To our best knowledge, concurrent mailbox behaviors are tackled in the following (parts of) specifications:

Base IMAP

The base IMAP4 specification has few explicit mentions of concurrent mailbox access, but does talk about re-synchronizing disconnected clients, which can be seen as a restricted form of concurrent access. It defines mechanisms for assigning IDs to emails (UIDNEXT/UIDVALIDITY) and associated properties which can be extrapolated to concurrent contexts. This is relevant when concurrently adding new emails to a mailbox. After an email has been added to a mailbox it cannot be modified, so there are no issues with reading emails concurrently.

The improvements that we will talk about in this post are related to these aspects of the base IMAP specification.

As an additional complication, IMAP defines in fact two (!) email-numbering systems. One of these has the drawback that deleting an email can invalidate email IDs used in concurrent commands. This is purely a quirk of a numbering system that can nowadays be considered legacy, but must still be supported. This issue is not acknowledged in the base IMAP specification, leaving a class of problematic behaviors completely unspecified, but is later addressed in an informational RFC which specifies what to do in such cases.

Aerogramme's latest release includes changes and bugfixes to make sure that we follow the recommendations of this informational RFC, but we won't enter into the details of these legacy quirks in this post.

扩展

Email flags can be modified concurrently, but the base IMAP specification does not specify a mechanism for clients to coordinate around flag changes. This is done in the later CONDSTORE specification that extends IMAP with mechanisms to coordinate flag changes across concurrent connections. Aerogramme has preliminary support for CONDSTORE, but we disabled it in the last release, as we found out it needs a redesign to be nicer to email clients1.

A later specification further extends IMAP and CONDSTORE by adding a more general mechanism (QRESYNC) for synchronizing all mailbox changes across concurrent sessions. Aerogramme does not supports QRESYNC at the moment2.

Context: Concurrency in Aerogramme

On top of the complexity carried by the IMAP specification, Aerogramme's distributed infrastructure comes with its own challenges. Not only we need to think about concurrency at the IMAP protocol level, but also internally in Aerogramme: how do we handle concurrent changes to the server internal data storage? Can we simply take a lock or a transaction over mailbox data each time we need to update it, serializing all concurrent updates? The answer is no: things are a bit more complicated...

Recall that Aerogramme is a distributed IMAP server. A typical Aerogramme deployment looks like this:

In this schema, A nodes are Aerogramme instances running on separate servers. Running multiple Aerogramme nodes provides fault-tolerance: even if some of the nodes crash, the Aerogramme cluster stays operational as long as one node remains available. When an email client (a C node) connects to the "Aerogramme cluster" (the dashed potato), it can open a connection to any of the Aerogramme nodes, depending on what kind of load-balancing is implemented.

Aerogramme nodes do not talk to each other directly and do not store data themselves. Instead, they connect a shared Garage cluster (itself geo-distributed with fault-tolerance properties) which stores data for the whole Aerogramme cluster (emails, mailbox state, etc.).

This means that an Aerogramme node deals with concurrency at two levels. It must handle concurrent connections from email clients to a mailbox, as we explained before. But it must also handle concurrent changes made by other Aerogramme nodes to the data stored in Garage. These concurrent accesses must be coordinated properly so that the Aerogramme cluster exposes a consistent view of a mailbox (according to IMAP's consistency requirements), even when connecting concurrently to different nodes of the Aerogramme cluster.

A central challenge in Aerogramme's design is that Garage does not provide locks, transactions, or anything that would require distributed consensus between Garage nodes. This is by design, and it allows Garage and Aerogramme to perform well even with non-negligible latency between nodes. The consequence for Aerogramme is that its nodes cannot simply reason on their shared data as if it was updated sequentially. The approach used by Aerogramme instead—a convergent operation log—is a central part of its design. We'll talk more below on how we adjusted the consistency properties provided by Garage when storing that operation log.

Testing the consistency of email numbering in Aerogramme

A basic IMAP mechanism is assigning IDs to emails when they are added into a mailbox. Adding emails concurrently can already make it tricky to assign these IDs. Our first step was to find a way of testing this case and to fix any bugs that we would find.

For context, IMAP specifies that each email in a mailbox must be assigned a UID: a number that identifies it uniquely. UIDs are assigned in increasing order; this allows clients to check if new emails have been added by checking the value of the mailbox "next UID". On top of that, IMAP also allows the server to renumber the emails with different UIDs. When this happens, the IMAP server must increase the value of UIDVALIDITY, a global integer counter attached to the mailbox. Now, in Aerogramme, increasing UIDVALIDITY is done in some cases when emails are added concurrently in the mailbox in a way that would assign conflicting UIDs; an unavoidable consequence of its distributed architecture.

From an IMAP client's perspective UIDVALIDITY must always increase monotonically. We also assume that this property must hold across all concurrent connections; although the specification does not say so explicitly, it is the most prudent assumption since a single client may open multiple connections to the same mailbox.

The logical next step is to setup a test bench to ensure that it holds in practice for Aerogramme! We deployed an Aerogramme cluster with three nodes, running on a simulated network with added latency between nodes. 然后：

  • we run two processes concurrently adding emails to a test mailbox, from two different nodes of the cluster. This is enough to trigger UID assignation conflicts, forcing Aerogramme to renumber emails and increase UIDVALIDITY;
  • at the same time, we run a checker for our property: a program that reads UIDVALIDITY from two different nodes of the cluster and checks that the second value read is greater or equal to the first one.

Running Aerogramme on this test bench found state synchronization bugs: bugs showing that Aerogramme’s distributed state (stored in Garage) was not always properly synchronized between nodes and concurrent sessions. Amusingly, most of these bugs were not specific to the IMAP logic related to UIDVALIDITY...

Fixing these synchronization bugs motivated a redesign of the internal read/update mailbox interface. In Aerogramme, the IMAP "business logic" accesses mailbox state stored in distributed storage using an abstract interface exposing a small number of operations. Before, these operations were the following (in pseudo-Rust):

// `self` is a handle to the storage backend for a mailbox.

/// Read the current state of the mailbox from remote storage.
fn get(&self) -> State

/// Push an operation that updates the mailbox to remote storage.
fn push_op(&self, op: Operation)

The synchronization bugs found during testing revealed that this interface is in fact error-prone and tricky to reason about:

  1. get could return outdated values; this is because rebuilding mailbox state from remote storage can be expensive, so get internally maintained a cache which could get stale;
  2. doing let s1 = mailbox.get(); ...; let s2 = mailbox.get(); is a trap. In this case, s2 imports unknown operations pushed concurrently from other clients. In most cases this is not what we want, as IMAP commands must generally behave as if they operated on a "snapshot" of the mailbox taken as a single point in time;
  3. push_op modifies the state, but if we need the mailbox state with the operation we just pushed, we have to call get (and thus likely fall into the trap described in 2.).

The solution was to redesign Aerogramme's mailbox state interface to provide more control over state synchronization: reading concurrent changes from storage becomes a separate operation, laying the following interface:

// `self` is now a thread-local view of the state of a mailbox.
// It is local to a given client connection.
// (As an optimization, it internally pools ressources with other
// views of the same mailbox.)

/// Return the local view of the mailbox maintained by `self`.
/// Does not read remote storage.
fn get(&self) -> State

/// Push an operation that updates the mailbox.
/// Update both the local view and remote storage.
fn push_op(&mut self, op: Operation)

/// Synchronize the local view of the mailbox.
/// Read remote storage and imports all changes into the local view. 
fn sync(&mut self)

This new interface separates local reasoning about mailbox contents from synchronization. This makes it easier to write the IMAP logic in a way that is "obviously correct". Plainly speaking, this interface provides "local" views of mailbox state, where a view (denoted as self above) is specific to a client connection. Then, get and push_op operate on the local view with sequential semantics and are both fast; and calls to sync mark explicitly the places in the code where we have to think about concurrent changes. (Note that push_op synchronously updates remote storage, so there is no risk of losing write by forgetting to run sync.)

Notice that the design of this interface reflects the high-level distributed architecture that we described in the previous section. For instance, an implementation of the interface needs to "merge" the operations pushed concurrently with push_op when they are put together in distributed storage, in a way that is consistent with local views; this is backed by the "convergent operation log" mentioned earlier and domain-specific logic3. Note that this interface offers no transactional or lock-like operations; matching Garage's lack of consistency primitives.

Most of the changes described here were part of Aerogramme 0.4, with in particular #129 implementing the refactoring of the state synchronization interface.

"Monotonic Reads" Consistency for Garage K2V

Talking about consistency guarantees in Aerogramme raises the question: what are the consistency guarantees provided by Garage, its storage backend?

This question is most relevant for Garage K2V, a NoSQL-inspired key-value store, which is used to store mailbox state as an operation log. (Garage K2V is experimental and was added in Garage for the needs of Aerogramme.) Mailbox state describes (among other things) email numbering, and as we've seen before, we want this information to be properly synchronized between Aerogramme nodes.

Garage K2V provides read-after-write consistency4: this guarantees that as soon as a write is acknowledged by Garage, any subsequent read will see the update made by the write. In terms of Aerogramme's state synchronization interface, after running push_op(op);, this guarantees that sync(); get() returns a state that includes op on any Aerogramme node.

However, it turns out that read-after-write consistency alone is not enough for Aerogramme. Let's think of the fact that UIDVALIDITY needs to increase monotonically according to the IMAP specification. This means that calling sync(); get() twice on any two Aerogramme nodes must return a state that is more recent the second time than the first. In other words, when making several reads to Garage K2V in sequence, we must not see time go backward. This means that, to ensure consistency of the UIDVALIDITY counter, Aerogramme needs Garage K2V to guarantee an additional consistency property called monotonic reads!

As a result we have extended Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads consistency. Luckily, the design of Garage makes it possible to provide monotonic reads at only a small performance cost. For a reference, Martin Kleppmann's Designing data-intensive applications (in particular Chapter 9, "Linearizability and quorums") helps understanding which scenarios lead to non-monotonic reads in a quorum-based architecture like Garage's, and what to implement to guarantee monotonic reads.

To experimentally validate our changes, we first built a test bench that triggers non-monotonic reads on stock K2V. Reproducing non-monotonic reads requires variable network delays, so we deployed a Garage cluster with 3 nodes, on a simulated network with delay between cluster nodes. This test setup allows observing non-monotonic reads, by running:

  • a writer program that writes increasing integer values (0, 1, 2, etc.);
  • a reader program that performs two reads in sequence from two different nodes of the cluster, and checks that it reads an integer that is greater on the second read than on the first read.

We then modified Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads by default, by implementing "synchronous read repair". We validated that we cannot observe non-monotonic reads anymore on our test bench, while they could be observed before this change: a good sanity check.

This change in Garage K2V ensures that there are no scenarios in which a precise combination of network delays in the cluster results in an IMAP client observing non-increasing values of UIDVALIDITY. One could argue that this is unlikely to happen in practice; and indeed, we could not reproduce it with our simple-minded test bench: while we could observe non-monotonic reads with Garage K2V alone, we could not observe non-monotonic UIDVALIDITY on a full Garage+Aerogramme deployment with the same testing methodology. Nevertheless, we want Aerogramme to rest on strong, correct foundations as much as possible; eliminating a rare but possible cause of bugs was fully worth the effort.

The work described here was made available as part of Garage 2.4.0; it required no specific change in Aerogramme itself.

We designed Aerogramme to be part of a low-tech computing stack meant to be robust and reliable when hosted outside of data-centers, and Aerogramme's geo-distributed design is part of the answer. In the future, we hope to expand on the values and high-level ideas behind Aerogramme; this will have to be for an other blogpost...
